newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan economy grew steadily in Oct-Dec quarter.
newsitem.headline: Japan economy grew steadily in Oct-Dec quarter.

text.p: Japan posted steady economic growth in the three months to the end of December and in calendar 1996, making it "highly likely" the nation will meet its target of 2.5 percent growth for this fiscal year, the government said on Thursday.

The nation's gross domestic product (GDP) -- total output of goods and services minus net income from overseas production -- rose a real 1.0 percent in the October-December period from the previous quarter, or an annualised 3.9 percent.
This compared with a revised quarter-on-quarter GDP rise of 0.3 percent for the July to September quarter.

In calendar 1996, the nation's GDP -- a closely watched pointer to the health of the economy -- rose a real 3.6 percent from the previous year after a revised figure of 1.4 percent growth in 1995, the Economic Planning Agency (EPA) said.

Economists polled by Reuters ahead of the announcement had predicted, on average, that October-December GDP would rise by 0.8 percent quarter-on-quarter. The forecasts had ranged from 0.3 percent to 1.2 percent growth. They had expected GDP to grow by more than three percent for calendar 1996.
An EPA official told reporters that Japan's economic growth would slow in the early part of fiscal 1997/98 from April 1, but would pick up in the latter half of the year.
"A slowing down is likely, but it will be temporary and the economy will return to steadier growth in the latter half of the year," EPA Vice Minister Shimpei Nukaya said.
Nukaya also said that the Japanese economy was highly likely to achieve a government target of 2.5 percent growth for fiscal 1996/97 to March 31.
Japan is tightening its government purse strings in an effort to get its big budget deficit under control, and will raise its three-percent sales tax to five percent from April 1.
The moves have raised concern in the United States that Japan's trade surplus is poised to swell as the nation tries to export its way out of domestic economic trouble.
Some economists said the latest data showed the economy was stronger than many pessimists feared, but added that export growth helped by a weak yen accounted for much of that strength.

"These numbers show that the economy probably has a little more momentum than most people thought up until now. Companies are investing more, and they aren't completely irrational," Kenneth Courtis, chief economist at Deutsche Bank Group Asia, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).

"As you look ahead, with the government slowing down domestic growth through these higher taxes, my sense is that export growth is going to be even stronger in the rest of this year. That's what is going to drive the economy -- exports and capital investment which is related to exports," Courtis added.

Others said, however, that more data would be needed to confirm that the recovery would remain on track. "We're still waiting for April-June (data)," said Peter Morgan, an economist at HSBC James Capel Japan.
